lead: A pump, turbine or pipe rarely holds a fixed mass: fluid crosses its boundary all the time. For an open system at steady state, mass in equals mass out, and the energy carried in by the streams plus the heat added equals the energy carried out plus the shaft work delivered. The bookkeeping must include the work that pushes each stream across the boundary, and that push work turns internal energy into enthalpy. The result is the steady-flow energy equation, used for turbines, compressors, nozzles and every control volume in a process plant.
prereq: You need: 1.3 for work and heat crossing a boundary, and 1.5 for ΔU = Q − W in a closed system.

blocks.text: A control volume is a chosen region of space. Its boundary may be a real casing or an imaginary surface across a pipe. Fluid crosses the boundary, so the control volume is an open system. In steady flow, properties at each fixed point inside and on the boundary do not change with time, so the mass inside stays constant even though fluid keeps moving through, and mass entering equals mass leaving. For one inlet 1 and one outlet 2, ṁ₁ = ṁ₂ = ṁ. Steady flow is not the same as no flow: a turbine at constant load is steady, while its start-up is not.

blocks.where: ṁ is mass flow rate in kg/s; in and out mark streams entering and leaving the control volume.

blocks.text: A stream carries energy in three forms per kilogram: internal energy u, kinetic energy c²/2 and potential energy gz, where c is the stream speed in m/s (this unit writes speed as c so that v stays specific volume). It also carries flow work. To push one kilogram into the control volume, the fluid behind it does work Pv, with P and v the pressure and specific volume of that stream where it enters. At the outlet the control volume does the work P₂v₂ to push its kilogram out. Each stream's flow work joins that same stream's internal energy, so every stream carries its own enthalpy h = u + Pv, worked out at its own pressure and specific volume.

blocks.where: h is specific enthalpy in kJ/kg; u is specific internal energy in kJ/kg; P is pressure in kPa; v is specific volume in m³/kg, so Pv is in kJ/kg. Pv is flow work, not shaft work.

blocks.text: With Q positive into the control volume and W<sub>s</sub> (shaft power) positive out of it, the steady-flow energy equation for any number of streams is:
Q − W<sub>s</sub> = Σṁ<sub>out</sub>(h + c²/2 + gz) − Σṁ<sub>in</sub>(h + c²/2 + gz)
blocks.where: Q is the heat rate into the control volume in kW; W<sub>s</sub> is the shaft power delivered by it in kW; ṁ is mass flow rate in kg/s; c is speed in m/s; g = 9.81 m/s²; z is elevation in m. Each bracket is energy per kg; multiply by ṁ in kg/s to get kW, after converting c²/2 with 1 kJ/kg = 1000 m²/s². Some syllabi call this the control-volume energy balance.

blocks.text: For one inlet and one outlet with the same ṁ, divide by ṁ. Here q = Q/ṁ and w<sub>s</sub> = W<sub>s</sub>/ṁ are heat in and shaft work out per kilogram, and subscript 1 is the inlet, 2 the outlet. The equation says: heat in minus shaft work out equals the rise in enthalpy, kinetic energy and potential energy of each kilogram between inlet and outlet.
q − w<sub>s</sub> = (h₂ − h₁) + (c₂² − c₁²)/2 + g(z₂ − z₁)
blocks.where: q and w<sub>s</sub> are in kJ/kg; h in kJ/kg; c in m/s (divide the c² term by 1000 for kJ/kg); z in m.

blocks.text: Neglect Δke or Δpe only after you estimate them. A speed change from 60 to 120 m/s gives Δke = 5.4 kJ/kg, small beside a steam enthalpy drop of hundreds of kJ/kg; in a nozzle, however, Δke is the main output. In a turbine h falls and Ws leaves; in a compressor Ws enters (negative) and h rises. A heat loss makes Q negative. The first law does not say Q = Ws: it says Q − Ws equals the energy carried out by the flow minus the energy carried in. Nozzles, compressors and throttling are worked out in 1.8.

When a tank fills or empties, the mass and energy inside change with time, so the storage term stays in. With kinetic and potential energy neglected, the mass and energy balances of the control volume are:
dm<sub>cv</sub>/dt = Σṁ<sub>in</sub> − Σṁ<sub>out</sub>;   d(mu)<sub>cv</sub>/dt = Q − W + Σṁ<sub>in</sub> h<sub>in</sub> − Σṁ<sub>out</sub> h<sub>out</sub>
blocks.where: m<sub>cv</sub> and u are the mass and specific internal energy inside the control volume; the streams still carry enthalpy h; Q and W are rates in kW.

blocks.text: Fill an evacuated, insulated, rigid tank from a supply line whose state stays fixed: Q = 0, W = 0, nothing leaves, so integrating gives m₂u₂ = m₂h<sub>line,</sub> that is u₂ = h<sub>line</sub>. For an ideal gas with constant heat capacities, c<sub>v</sub> T₂ = c<sub>p</sub> T<sub>line,</sub> so T₂ = γT<sub>line</sub>: the gas in the tank ends hotter than the line, because the flow work of every kilogram pushed in is stored as internal energy.

examples.question: Steam enters a turbine at h₁ = 3200 kJ/kg and c₁ = 60 m/s. It leaves at h₂ = 2600 kJ/kg and c₂ = 120 m/s. The mass flow rate is 2.0 kg/s and the casing loses 50 kW of heat. Neglect potential energy. Find the shaft power.
steps: Steady-flow energy equation for one inlet and one outlet: Q − W<sub>s</sub> = ṁ[(h₂ − h₁) + (c₂² − c₁²)/2].
Kinetic term in kJ/kg: (c₂² − c₁²)/2 = (120² − 60²)/2 = (14 400 − 3600)/2 = 5400 J/kg = 5.4 kJ/kg.
Energy change per kg: −600 + 5.4 = −594.6 kJ/kg; times ṁ: 2.0 × (−594.6) = −1189.2 kW.
Heat loss is negative heat input, Q = −50 kW. Then −50 − W<sub>s</sub> = −1189.2, so W<sub>s</sub> = 1189.2 − 50 = 1139.2 kW.
examples.answer: The turbine delivers 1139.2 kW (about 1.14 MW) of shaft power.

examples.question: An evacuated, insulated, rigid tank of 0.50 m³ is connected to an air line at 600 kPa and 300 K. The valve is opened and closed when the tank pressure reaches 600 kPa. Treat air as an ideal gas with γ = 1.4 and R = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K). Find the final temperature and the mass of air in the tank.
steps: Control volume: the tank. Q = 0 (insulated), W = 0 (rigid, no shaft), no outflow, and the tank starts empty, so m₁ = 0.
Mass balance: m₂ = m<sub>in</sub>. Energy balance integrated over the filling: m₂u₂ − 0 = m<sub>in</sub> h<sub>line,</sub> so u₂ = h<sub>line</sub>.
Ideal gas, constant heat capacities, both measured from 0 K: c<sub>v</sub> T₂ = c<sub>p</sub> T<sub>line,</sub> so T₂ = γT<sub>line</sub> = 1.4 × 300 = 420 K.
Mass from the ideal-gas law: m₂ = P₂V/(RT₂) = 600 × 0.50/(0.287 × 420) = 300/120.54 = 2.489 kg.
examples.answer: The air in the tank ends at 420 K (147 °C), and the tank holds 2.49 kg.

traps: Using u instead of h for a flowing stream: the flow work Pv is already in h. For a turbine or compressor, h is the property you look up in steam tables.
Dropping kinetic energy because it looks small: convert m²/s² to kJ/kg by dividing by 1000, then compare with Δh. 100 m/s gives 5 kJ/kg, not 5000 kJ/kg.
Sign slip on Q and W<sub>s</sub>: Q is positive into the control volume; W<sub>s</sub> is positive out. A 50 kW heat loss is Q = −50 kW, not +50 kW.
Treating flow work as shaft work: Pv is not W<sub>s</sub>. W<sub>s</sub> crosses the boundary through a shaft; Pv crosses with the fluid.

Applying the steady-flow equation to a tank that is filling or emptying. Then the mass and energy inside change, and the storage term d(mu)<sub>cv</sub>/dt stays in; for filling an empty insulated tank, u₂ = h<sub>line,</sub> not h₂ = h<sub>line</sub>.

quiz.q: Write the steady-flow mass balance for several inlets and outlets.
quiz.a: Σṁ<sub>in</sub> = Σṁ<sub>out,</sub> where ṁ is mass flow rate in kg/s.

quiz.q: Why does enthalpy appear instead of internal energy in the steady-flow energy equation?
quiz.a: A flowing stream carries flow work Pv as well as internal energy u. The sum u + Pv is h, so h groups both terms.

quiz.q: For one stream, q = 20 kJ/kg, w<sub>s</sub> = 0, Δke = 0 and Δpe = 0. Find Δh.
quiz.a: q − w<sub>s</sub> = Δh, so Δh = 20 kJ/kg.

quiz.q: Steam has h1 = 3000 kJ/kg and h2 = 2700 kJ/kg. Kinetic and potential changes are negligible and Q = 0. The mass flow is 1.5 kg/s. Find W<sub>s</sub>.
quiz.a: Q − W<sub>s</sub> = ṁ(h2 − h1). 0 − W<sub>s</sub> = 1.5(2700 − 3000) = −450 kW, so W<sub>s</sub> = 450 kW.

quiz.q: A student uses u instead of h for a steam turbine. At the inlet P₁v₁ = 330 kJ/kg; at the outlet P₂v₂ = 120 kJ/kg. Kinetic, potential and heat terms are negligible. What error results?
quiz.a: The true work is w<sub>s</sub> = h₁ − h₂ = (u₁ − u₂) + (P₁v₁ − P₂v₂). Using u leaves out P₁v₁ − P₂v₂ = 330 − 120 = 210 kJ/kg, so the computed work is 210 kJ/kg too low for every kilogram of steam.

quiz.q: Why is Q = W<sub>s</sub> wrong for a turbine even when Δke and Δpe are neglected?
quiz.a: The flow carries enthalpy in and out. The balance is Q − W<sub>s</sub> = ṁ(h2 − h1). The enthalpy drop, not Q alone, supplies the shaft work.

quiz.q: An evacuated insulated tank is filled from a helium line at 300 K (γ = 1.67). Find the final gas temperature.
quiz.a: u₂ = h<sub>line,</sub> so T₂ = γT<sub>line</sub> = 1.67 × 300 = 501 K.

beyond: Not for the exam. Dynamic plant simulators keep the storage term through start-up, shutdown and load changes. Exergy analysis uses the same control volume to locate lost work, and CFD writes these balances for millions of tiny control volumes. Search next for transient tank filling and exergy of a stream.
